'''Erhard Schmidt''' (13 January 1876 – 6 December 1959) was a [[Baltic German]] mathematician whose work significantly influenced the direction of mathematics in the twentieth century.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Schmidt}}</ref> Schmidt was born in [[Tartu]] ({{langx|de|link=no|Dorpat}}), in the [[Governorate of Livonia]] (now [[Estonia]]).

== Mathematics ==
His advisor was [[David Hilbert]]<ref name="Hilbert"/> and he was awarded his doctorate from [[University of Göttingen]] in 1905. His doctoral dissertation was entitled ''{{lang|de|Entwickelung willkürlicher Funktionen nach Systemen vorgeschriebener}}'' and was a work on [[integral equations]].<ref name="Hilbert"/> Together with [[David Hilbert]] he made important contributions to [[functional analysis]]. [[Ernst Zermelo]] credited conversations with Schmidt for the idea and method for his classic 1904 proof of the [[Well-ordering theorem]] from an "[[Axiom of choice]]", which has become an integral part of modern [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory|set theory]].<ref>{{harvnb|Zermelo|1904|pages=514, 516}}.</ref>

After the war, in 1948, Schmidt founded and became the first editor-in-chief of the journal ''{{lang|de|[[Mathematische Nachrichten]]}}''.<ref name="mactutor"/>

== National Socialism ==
During [[World War II]] Schmidt held positions of authority at the [[University of Berlin]] and had to carry out various [[Nazi]] resolutions against the Jews—a job that he apparently did not do well, since he was criticized at one point for not understanding the "[[Jewish question]]". At the celebration of Schmidt's 75th birthday in 1951 a prominent Jewish mathematician, [[Hans Freudenthal]], who had survived the Nazi years, spoke of the difficulties that Schmidt faced during that period without criticism.<ref name="mactutor"/> Schmidt was, however, a conservative and a nationalist, and, in 1938, defended [[Hitler]] after [[Kristallnacht]], telling Jewish mathematician [[Issai Schur]]: "Suppose we had to fight a war to rearm Germany, [[Anschluss|unite]] with [[Austria]], liberate the [[Territory of the Saar Basin|Saar]] and the [[Sudetenland|German part]] of [[Czechoslovakia]]. Such a war would have cost us half a million young men. But everybody would have admired our victorious leader. Now, Hitler has sacrificed half a million Jews and has achieved great things for Germany. I hope some day you will be recompensed but I am still grateful to Hitler".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Segal |first=Sanford L. |author-link=Sanford L. Segal |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xa8CNCyohBQC&pg=PA358 |title=Mathematicians Under the Nazis |date=2003 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-00451-8 |page=358 |language=en}}</ref>
